title: Who Pays for AI?
subtitle: The environmental costs of data centers and the choices that distribute them
question: How do choices about power source, cooling, and cost sharing affect the environmental costs of AI data centers and the energy bills of nearby households?
thesis: Responsible AI growth needs technical choices that lower resource use and policy choices that share the remaining costs fairly.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: As an AI answer appears on a screen, there are real buildings and equipment running in the background to make it happen. Servers use power, cooling systems remove heat, and utilities connect data centers to shared grids. People who use AI may live far from the places that supply these resources. This raises my main driving question: how do choices about power source, cooling, and cost sharing affect the environmental costs of AI data centers and the energy bills of nearby households? My answer is that responsible AI growth needs two kinds of choices: technical choices that lower resource use, and policy choices that share the remaining costs fairly.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centers used 485 terawatt-hours of electricity worldwide in 2025. Its central projection reaches about 950 terawatt-hours in 2030 [1]. These figures cover all data center services, not just AI. The future number is a projection, not a certainty. Growth on that scale would put pressure on electricity supply, power lines, and cooling systems. Decisions about where to build and who should pay therefore belong in the discussion of AI’s environmental costs.

This project shows how a data center’s electricity supply, cooling system, and grid upgrade agreement affect resource use and household energy costs in lower and higher income communities. I explore the question with an interactive simulation of a fictional data center. Published research provides the accounting methods and explains why the choices matter. The capacity, cooling values, household budgets, and cost allocation are simplified assumptions. The model shows relationships between these choices; it does not predict what will happen in a real city.

sections.title: Electricity Use
paragraphs: A data center needs power to run, and its carbon emissions depend in part on how that power is made. A lower carbon source can reduce emissions while leaving the need for power plants, power lines, and cooling in place. This is why my model separates the amount of electricity from its source. Berkeley Lab estimates that US data centers used 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, about 4.4 percent of national electricity use, and projects a range of 325–580 terawatt-hours by 2028 [2]. The range reflects different assumptions about equipment, operation, and cooling. It is not a prediction for the neighborhood in this simulation.

Masanet and colleagues give a different picture of the recent past. From 2010 to 2018, global data center computing workloads grew more than sixfold while electricity use grew about 6 percent. Improvements in equipment, utilization, and the shift toward larger cloud facilities helped offset the growth [8]. But I do not think past results mean that today’s AI growth will follow the same path. Berkeley Lab identifies growing use of accelerated servers as an important driver of rising demand [2]. Together, these studies show why efficiency matters without guaranteeing that total demand will stay flat. The earlier study describes global historical trends; the later report models US demand, so they are not a single continuous forecast.

These sources frame the electricity part of my simulation. Rather than guessing how fast AI demand will grow, I keep computing work fixed and multiply total facility electricity by an emissions factor. This isolates the effect of the power source and follows the accounting method described in EPA guidance [6]. The factors, 400 and 50 kilograms of CO₂e per megawatt-hour, are illustrative higher- and lower-carbon inputs. They are not measured supplies for this site or guarantees about a particular technology. The model leaves out hardware manufacturing, construction, and backup generators, so it covers only part of the environmental cost.

sections.title: Cooling and Water Use
sections.takeaway: A tradeoff between water and power
paragraphs: Cooling is a second environmental cost, and the two cooling methods in my model trade water for power. Mytton explains that cooling needs depend on local conditions and that onsite water figures leave out water used to generate electricity [3]. In my simulation, dry cooling uses less water but more power than evaporative cooling. Berkeley Lab discusses this possible tradeoff [2]. The size of the difference is chosen for this example, not a rule for every facility.

Research on US data centers shows that both location and power supply affect environmental costs [7]. The same amount of water matters more where water is scarce. Because my model leaves out watersheds, seasons, and drought, it reports liters without assigning a water stress score. Dry cooling alone does not prove that a data center has no effect on water systems. In this scenario it shifts some demand from onsite water to the electricity system, with an emissions effect that depends on the power source.

The input ledger below makes the comparison reproducible. A 10-megawatt computing load running at 80 percent utilization for 8,760 hours uses 70,080 MWh a year before cooling and other overhead. Total facility electricity is 1.20 times that amount with evaporative cooling and 1.35 times with dry cooling. Direct water use is 1.20 or 0.02 liters per kilowatt-hour of computing electricity. These are fixed teaching inputs, not measurements from a particular facility. Users choose the power source, cooling method, income profile, and cost-sharing rule; the other values stay fixed.

The distinction between computing electricity and total facility electricity matters. The overhead multiplier includes power used beyond the computing equipment, while the water intensity here is applied to computing electricity. A common denominator makes the comparison easier to follow. Changing the denominator or leaving out indirect water could change how a facility looks, even without changing its operation. The ledger therefore states both the number and what it measures [2][3].

sections.title: Income and Cost Sharing
sections.takeaway: The same bill. A different burden.
paragraphs: The third element is household budgets, because the same bill has a different weight for families with different incomes. ACEEE defines energy burden as “the percentage of household income spent on energy bills” [4]. This is why my model compares lower and higher incomes using the same energy bill: annual incomes of $30,000 and $100,000 and a yearly bill of $1,800. These are comparison values, not survey results. Keeping the bill the same makes the effect of income easier to see.

A reported example adds a household perspective. Michelle Jarboe’s 2026 News 5 Cleveland report follows Keith and Cheryl Kasnik in Perry Township. Their electric bill exceeded $500 in December and $600 in February; December–March spending was about 60 percent higher than a year earlier. The nearby operation was a cryptocurrency mining campus, not an identified AI facility. The article does not establish how much of this household’s increase it caused [10]. I use this case to illustrate affordability concerns, not to calibrate the simulation or assume the Kasniks’ income.

Rules can change who carries infrastructure risk. In July 2025, PUCO ordered a data center tariff for AEP Ohio, stating that the settlement “safeguards other non-data center customers from cost-shifting risks” [5]. Such protections depend on the utility, contract, and customers covered. Jarboe also describes a stalled June 2026 reform effort, House Bill 646, and disagreements over tax breaks [10]. This is a dated policy example, not a claim about the bill’s current status. A tariff cannot simply be treated as a guarantee that every household’s electricity bill will fall.

The simulation represents cost sharing with three choices: the company pays, residents pay, or each pays half. The assumed upgrade costs $20 million, spread over ten years and 10,000 households. This gives annual household charges of $0, $200, or $100, without interest. The household charge pays for the modeled upgrade, not for the data center’s electricity purchases. These round numbers make the allocation easy to compare; they do not forecast a real utility bill.

This choice applies Meadows’s idea of leverage points. Her framework places system rules above changes to individual numerical parameters as potential places to intervene [9]. Applied here, an agreement about who must fund infrastructure changes how costs are allocated across households. This is my application of her systems framework, not a data center case from her essay. Changing income or the funding rule affects household burden while the facility’s electricity and cooling settings stay the same.

sections.title: Results and Limitations
paragraphs: Under the stated assumptions, the simulation gives three important results. Choosing the lower carbon source reduces operational electricity emissions to one-eighth of the grid scenario, an 87.5 percent reduction, while electricity demand stays unchanged. Dry cooling reduces direct water use by about 98.3 percent but raises total facility electricity by 12.5 percent. The $1,800 bill is a 6 percent burden for the $30,000 household and 1.8 percent for the $100,000 household. The residents-pay option raises these to about 6.67 percent and 2.00 percent. These are calculated comparisons, not research measurements.

Each result points back to my argument. A cleaner power source lowers one environmental cost without lowering the demand placed on the grid. Dry cooling changes the balance between water and power. Because the model holds the existing household bill fixed, only the cost-sharing rule changes the added household charge. Lower resource use and fair cost sharing are separate problems. Solving one does not automatically solve the other.

The model’s limits are also clear. Fixed inputs leave out future growth, changes in equipment use, hot days, and peak demand. It does not connect the data center’s electricity consumption to household electricity prices, so the extra power used by dry cooling never appears as an additional residential electricity charge. It does not estimate jobs, tax revenue, land impacts, supply chains, or AI’s possible social benefits. It cannot weigh all of AI’s gains against its costs or support a complete judgment about any real facility.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: My question asked how choices about power, cooling, and cost sharing affect the environmental costs of AI and the costs paid by nearby households. The model’s answer is that these choices address different parts of the problem. A lower carbon power source lowers emissions without lowering electricity demand. Dry cooling lowers direct water use but raises electricity use under these assumptions. A cost-sharing rule decides who funds the modeled upgrade, and energy burden shows why the same charge matters more to a lower-income household.

The household reporting and the Ohio tariff bring this question beyond equipment choices. Residents need clear information about resource demand, financial responsibilities, and the reach of any promised protections. Responsible AI growth needs both lower resource use and fair cost sharing. Before calling a project sustainable, we should ask what it requires from the environment and whose interests are represented when its terms are set.
